Pacific red snapper (Lutjanus peru) achieves a maximum recorded fork length of 95 centimeters [Li = 95 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger-bodied lutjanids inhabiting the eastern Pacific continental shelf. This asymptotic dimension, derived from extensive fisheries-independent surveys along the Mexican coast, represents the theoretical upper boundary of somatic growth for the species under prevailing environmental conditions. Comparative morphological analyses indicate that individuals approaching this length are relatively rare in contemporary catches, likely reflecting the cumulative impact of sustained fishing pressure on older age classes. Field records further demonstrate that the fork length at which 50 percent of females have attained sexual maturity is 38 centimeters [Lp = 38 centimeters], a benchmark that corresponds to a fundamental transition in energy use, where resources are increasingly directed toward reproductive development rather than further body growth. This pubertal length is notably modest relative to the ultimate size potential of the species, suggesting that Lutjanus peru follows an energetically conservative strategy wherein reproductive capability is acquired well before the cessation of somatic growth, thereby maximizing lifetime fecundity.

The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva following eclosion, is approximately 0.00025 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00025 grams]. This minute initial mass is derived from an average egg diameter of 0.78 millimeters, which yields a spherical volume that, at a density consistent with marine teleost ova, translates into the observed neonatal weight. Such a diminutive starting point imposes stringent constraints on early larval survival, as the endogenous yolk reserves must sustain the prolarva through the period of mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding before the point of no return is crossed. The age at birth, defined as the interval from gamete fertilization to chorion rupture, is 6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days] under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C]. This developmental duration is consistent with the rapid embryogenesis observed in many tropical lutjanids, where elevated water temperatures accelerate cleavage, gastrulation, and organogenesis, thereby minimizing the pelagic egg stage and the associated risk of planktonic predation.

As post-settlement juveniles undergo somatic growth and progress toward reproductive maturity, the average body weight at puberty—that is, the mass corresponding to the fork length at puberty of 38 centimeters—is estimated at 728 grams [Wwp = 728 grams]. This value is derived from the species-specific length-weight relationship that describes the allometric scaling of mass with fork length across the entire size range of Lutjanus peru. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight attained by individuals that have reached the asymptotic fork length of 95 centimeters is 11061 grams [Wwi = 11061 grams], nearly fifteen times the mass at puberty, illustrating the substantial scope for continued somatic expansion after the onset of reproductive activity. This pronounced post-maturational growth is a hallmark of the indeterminate growth strategy characteristic of teleosts, wherein energy surplus beyond the demands of gonadal development and basal maintenance is directed toward increasing body size. The steep trajectory from pubertal to asymptotic mass underscores the species' capacity to occupy a broad trophic niche across its lifespan, shifting from a diet dominated by crustaceans during the juvenile stage to one increasingly composed of demersal fish and cephalopods as adults.

Field sampling of gravid females during the peak spawning season revealed a mean gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 5.8% [GSI = 5.8%] at the ambient water temperature of 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C]. The temperature-dependence of gonadal recrudescence is evident in the synchronization of spawning activity with seasonal thermal maxima, which in this species coincides with the summer months when sea surface temperatures consistently reach the 26.2 °C threshold.

Longevity data from otolith-based age estimation studies indicate that the maximum documented lifespan of Pacific red snapper is 16 years [am = 16 years], classifying Lutjanus peru as a moderately long-lived species among eastern Pacific lutjanids, with a life-history strategy that balances extended somatic growth and multiple annual spawning events against a background of natural mortality imposed by piscivory and episodic environmental variability at a temperature of 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C]. Consistent with the elevated metabolic demands associated with a warm-water existence, the age at birth of 6.5 days [ab = 6.5 days] at 26.2 °C represents a rapid embryogenic phase that is tightly coupled to the thermal optimum for larval development and survival at a temperature of 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C]. Collectively, these life-history parameters—rapid early ontogeny, moderate age at sexual maturation, substantial post-maturational growth, and a prolonged reproductive lifespan—position Lutjanus peru as a species with a balanced pace-of-life that is well-suited to the relatively stable, food-rich environments of the eastern Pacific continental margin.
